newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: TRADE SURPLUS JUMPS
Australia recorded a big surplus in international trade in goods and services in May.
Bureau of Statistics figures just released show the trade surplus rose to $873 million in May, a substantial increase on the $182-million surplus recorded in April.
However the results have been skewed by the sale of a Navy ship.
The Bureau of Statistics says exports of goods and services rose by 5 per cent in May, but this was largely attributable to the half billion dollar sale of the ANZAC frigate Te Kaha.
The surplus was also assisted by a 3 per cent fall in imports, with the biggest drop in purchases of business investment items.
AIRPORT LEASING PROCESS FINALISED
The Federal Government has finalised the process for the long term lease of the Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth airports, which take effect from midnight tonight.
Finance minister John Fahey says the Government has signed 50-year leases with the new operators, with an option of a further 49-years.
Mr Fahey says all three successful bidders are high quality, committed operators with international experience, who'll bring world's best practice to airport management and operation.
He says the first round of privatisation augurs well for the next phase, involving 15 smaller airports.
Mr Fahey says the process just completed indicates considerable interest in airports.
He says he expects a great deal of competition for the remaining airports and a very good return to the taxpayers at the conclusion of that process.
MINERS' UNION SAYS MINE DICING WITH DEATH
The coal miner's union says management of the Hunter Valley Mine in New South Wales is "dicing with death" by using unqualified staff to operate mining equipment.
The comments come as a strike enters its fourth week and as administrative staff are trained in the operation of trucks and loaders.
Rio Tinto, which owns the mine, claims it's losing $1-million a day because of the strike.
Mine General Manager Allan Davies says he has no other choice but to employ non-union staff in order to prevent further losses.
Mr Davies says 70 non-union staff have volunteered to learn how to use the equipment and are keen to get the mine operations back up and running.
He says the training is taking two weeks and is fully accredited.
But the miners' union says the move is an attempt to de-regulate health and safety standards in the open-cut mining industry.
The union's Mick Watson says the company is playing with the lives of its employees and the move could plunge the industry into chaos.
He says despite the training the staff lack the experience and qualifications to operate the machinery.
Meanwhile CFMEU president John Maitland says some workers at the mine have been threatened into operating the gear. The claims have been rejected by the mine's manager Allan Davies.
BANKER IN COURT ON INSIDER TRADING CHARGE
A Sydney Court has been told that a senior Sydney banker allegedly obtained crucial information from his employer about a planned takeover of transport group TNT last year.
The 36-year-old Macquarie Bank executive, Simon Hannes, is facing committal proceedings on a charge of insider trading.
Mr Hannes' employer, Macquarie Bank, was involved with the planned takeover of TNT by a Dutch group late last year.

The Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecution alleges although Mr Hannes' was not directly involved in the takeover, he had crucial information about the transaction through conversations with other employees and from documents in cabinets and on desks.
It's alleged he withdrew cash from various banks to buy TNT call options.
A decision is expected early this afternoon from Magistrate Deborah Sweeney on whether Mr Hannes will be committed to stand trial on the insider trading charge.
NATIONAL PROTESTS AGAINST CHILD CARE CUTS
Nationwide protests against cuts to subsidies for community-based child-care centres have begun with the laying of a wreath at John Howard's Sydney electoral office.
About 100 parents, children and child-care workers rallied outside the office and handed out stickers and leaflets to motorists, in protest at the cuts to operational subsidies for the centres.
Rallies and community forums are being held in all capital cities this morning to protest the subsidy withdrawals.
Aaron Magner of the Miscellaneous Workers' Union says the loss of the subsidies means each community-based child-care centre loses about $40,000 from today.
Mr Magner says that money will need to be made up by increasing fees for parents and cutting some quality care.
He says that means cutting services like nappy-changing services, hot meals, staff numbers and overall hours, all of which will be bad for the quality of child-care provided.
ETHICS COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER HIV VACCINE
The President of the Human Rights Commission, Sir Ronald Wilson, has agreed to head a special ethics committee in Melbourne to grapple with plans to use a potential HIV vaccine on healthy people.
The vaccine is based on a live HIV virus which comes from people who have not developed AIDS despite more than 15 years of HIV infection.
The HIV virus in those people was found to contain a deletion in one key gene.
The McFarlane Burnett Centre for Medical Research is laboratory testing the virus's potential as a vaccine.
Senior research fellow, Doctor Simon Kent, says live attenuated virus vaccines produce exactly the right immune response.
But even though it's much weaker than the original virus, there is nervousness about possible HIV infection in healthy people.
"It's a very thorny issue," Dr Kent said. "The ethics of doing those sort of trials are very difficult."
Dr Kent says trials will be done on individuals already infected with HIV but will also have to be done on HIV unaffected people.
The centre says Sir Ronald wilson will chair the special ethical committee to look at whether clinical trials can start.
